description:
Earth Trend Detectives | Seattle | Turning NASA Data into Action | Seattle Scope

We are Seattle Scope, a Seattle-based team for the challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" We turn NASA satellite data into visual stories about our changing Earth — from deforestation and urban heat to water and climate trends.
summary: Seattle-Scope is a web application built for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge. It shows how precipitation and root-zone soil moisture have changed from 1981 to 2025 in 39 cities across 6 continents, using NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data. A user picks a continent and a city and gets plain-language answers to the four challenge questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. The app also finds cities where the same variable moves in opposite directions, for example where rainfall stays stable but the soil becomes drier. This matters because rainfall alone does not tell us whether land is getting drier, and this affects farming, water planning and drought risk.
details:
What it does: For each city, Seattle-Scope shows annual precipitation and root-zone soil moisture (top ~1 m of soil) from 1981 to 2025. For each variable it reports the change per decade as a percentage of the city's average, a 95% confidence interval, a p-value, the number of years used, and a one-sentence verdict (for example, "significant decrease"). Users can compare two cities side by side. If both trends are significant and opposite, an OPPOSITE TRENDS badge appears. A continent overview lists the strongest opposite-trend pairs and groups cities with similar behaviour.

How it works: Monthly data from NASA POWER was collected for 39 cities using their coordinates, then cleaned and validated. It is stored as a CSV cache inside the repository, so the live app never waits for NASA. Monthly values are averaged into annual values (years with fewer than 9 valid months are dropped). The Mann-Kendall test checks whether a trend is statistically significant, and Sen's slope measures its size. For machine learning, a linear model with an annual cycle (scikit-learn) gives an indicative 10-year projection (2026-2035), and K-Means clustering groups cities with similar precipitation and soil-moisture changes. The project includes a Python FastAPI backend that serves the results as JSON. The current Vercel deployment serves the static HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend and uses the bundled CSV cache; the backend remains available for local development.

Benefits: It turns complex climate data into simple, honest answers. It says "no clear trend" when there is none and "n/a" where data does not exist (for example, soil moisture over ice). Any demo or synthetic data is always clearly labelled.

What we hope to achieve: To show that "less rain" and "drier soil" are not always the same story, and to make long-term Earth system trends easy to explore for students, communities and planners.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, GitHub, Vercel (hosting).

Limits: MERRA-2 is reanalysis (observations blended with a model), not a direct measurement. The projection is indicative only and is not a weather forecast or an official NASA climate projection. The project is not officially affiliated with NASA.
